Born into a Lahore industrial family and the longest-serving prime minister in Pakistan's history — across three non-consecutive terms, each one ending in his ousting — who is this politician and businessman?
Nawaz Sharif: Prime Minister of Pakistan (1990–1993; 1997–1999; 2013–2017)

A communist Eastern Bloc state founded in 1945, it launched a successful 1975 offensive against its southern rival before merging the next year into a single Socialist Republic — what was this country?
North Vietnam: Country in Southeast Asia (1945–1976)
Once Britain's youngest sitting MP — who crossed from Conservative to independent to Labour — this baronet then founded the British Union of Fascists in 1932. Who was he?
The first Carolingian to hold the Frankish throne, this son of Charles Martel began his reign in 751 after years as joint Mayor of the Palace with his brother — who was he?
Pepin the Short: King of the Franks from 751 to 768.
This ancient Indian king fought valiantly against Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BC, and was rewarded with an expanded realm despite his defeat — who is he?
A billionaire businessman who became Lebanon's first post-civil-war prime minister and helped rebuild Beirut, his 2005 assassination shook the country — who was he?
Rafic Hariri: Prime Minister of Lebanon (1992–1998; 2000–2004)

Fought from 1964 to 1979 in what would become independent Zimbabwe, this conflict pitted Ian Smith's white minority government against guerrilla forces led by Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo — what was it called?
Rhodesian Bush War: 1964–1979 conflict in Southern Africa.
He founded Electronic Data Systems and never carried a single state, yet his 1992 and 1996 runs were among the strongest third-party showings in U.S. history — which Texan businessman was it?
Ross Perot: American businessman and politician (1930–2019)

After publicizing the Gold Rush and founding San Francisco's first newspaper, this Latter-day Saint became California's first millionaire — before his vigilance-committee actions got him disfellowshipped — who was he?
Named after a 1968 Czechoslovak uprising, this brief South Korean democratization movement began the night President Park Chung Hee was assassinated in 1979 — what is it called?
Seoul Spring: Period of democratization in South Korea (1979–1980)

Led by the future Roman emperor Titus, an army encircled and breached the walls of this Jewish holy city, destroying the Second Temple after a bitter feud between rival factions cut off the population's own food supply — which historic event is this?
Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE): Part of the First Jewish–Roman War.
Stepping out of his family's iron-and-steel business and into Parliament, this Conservative dominated British politics between the wars, serving as prime minister three separate times — who was he?
Stanley Baldwin: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1923–1924; 1924–1929; 1935–1937)
Led by a man who declared himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, this 1850s Chinese theocratic state waged a 14-year war against the Qing dynasty — what was it?
Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: Theocratic monarchy in China (1851–1864)
Of African descent through his mother, this French Revolutionary Wars general was one of only a handful of men of color to command European troops as a general officer in that era — who is he?
A law professor with a doctorate from the London School of Economics, she became the first woman to serve as president of the Republic of China, from 2016 to 2024 — who is she?

Tsai Ing-wen: President of the Republic of China from 2016 to 2024. Following the DPP's defeat in the 2008 presidential election, Tsai was elected party chair, a position she held three times (2008–2012, 2014–2018, and 2020–2022).
Born in Turin, this ruler of Sardinia became the first king of a united Italy in 1861 and earned a nickname echoing an ancient Roman imperial title, 'Father of the Fatherland.' Who was he?
Victor Emmanuel II: King of Italy from 1861 to 1878.

Fought alongside a wider Georgian civil conflict, this early-1990s fight pitted government forces against separatists backed by North Caucasian militants, Cossacks, and the Russian military — which conflict?
War in Abkhazia (1992–1993): Conflict between Georgia and Abkhaz separatists.
After an evangelical conversion in 1785, this Yorkshire MP spent two decades leading the parliamentary fight that ended Britain's slave trade — who was he?
William Wilberforce: English politician and abolitionist (1759–1833)
What is this — “Aniconic representation of the Hindu goddess Shakti, consort of Shiva”?

Yoni: Aniconic representation of the Hindu goddess Shakti, consort of Shiva. Yoni (Sanskrit: योनि, IAST: yoni), sometimes called pindika, is an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu goddess Shakti.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four. Benjamin Banneker (November 9, 1731 – October 19, 1806) was an American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author.
Which one below was born first?

Omar Khayyam (born 1048) is the earliest of the four. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
Which one below was established earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four appeared first?
Lisp (programming language) (published 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Sally Ride is a physicist. Sally Kristen Ride (May 26, 1951–July 23, 2012) was an American astronaut and physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
James B. Conant is a chemist. James Bryant Conant (March 26, 1893 – February 11, 1978) was an American chemist, a President of Harvard University, and the first U.S.
What is the atomic number of Neon?
Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
In what year was Jim Ratcliffe born?
Jim Ratcliffe: Sir James Arthur Ratcliffe (born 18 October 1952) is a British billionaire, chemical engineer, and businessman.
In what year was Thales of Miletus born?
Thales of Miletus: Thales of Miletus ( THAY-leez; Ancient Greek: Θαλῆς; c. 626/623 – c. 548/545 BC) was an Ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher from Miletus in Ionia, Asia Minor.
In what year was Ada Lovelace born?
Ada Lovelace: Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
In what year did Neil Armstrong die?
Neil Armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
In what year did Wernher von Braun die?
Wernher von Braun: As a young man, von Braun worked in Nazi Germany's rocket development program.
In what year was Nitroglycerin discovered?
Nitroglycerin: It is combined with nitrocellulose to form double-based smokeless powder, used as a propellant in artillery and firearms since the 1880s.
In what year was Thallium discovered?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
Ceftriaxone: Pfizer. Ceftriaxone, sold under the brand name Rocephin, is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
In which country is Māori language?
Māori language: New Zealand. The southernmost member of the Austronesian language family, it is related to Cook Islands Māori, Tuamotuan, and Tahitian.
Who is credited with discovering Radium?
Radium: Marie Curie. Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
Who is credited with discovering Saccharin?
Saccharin: Constantin Fahlberg. Saccharin, also called saccharine, benzosulfimide, or E954, or used in saccharin sodium or saccharin calcium forms, is a non-nutritive artificial sweetener.
Who is credited with discovering Chlorine?
Chlorine: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, this thinker is often called the "father of economics" and is best known for "The Theory of Moral Sentiments" and "The Wealth of Nations" — who is it?
Adam Smith was Scottish economist and philosopher (1723–1790).
Once thought to be the last living species in its genus after a related 'sea' cousin went extinct, this North American mustelid now thrives as an invasive species in Europe — which animal?
American mink (Neogale vison) is a semiaquatic species of mustelid native to North America, though human introduction has expanded its range to many parts of Europe, Asia, and South America.
A physician who called medicine his lawful wife and literature his mistress, this Russian writer produced four stage classics and ranks among modernism's founders — who is he?
Anton Chekhov was Russian dramatist and author (1860–1904).

The third-largest member of its family behind the Siberian taimen and Pacific Chinook, this anadromous fish hatches in rivers, matures at sea, and changes color and appearance when it returns upstream to spawn — name this fish?
Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) is a species of ray-finned fish in the family Salmonidae.
This steroid medication treats conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis to asthma, and is also given before preterm birth to help speed a baby's lung development — what drug is it?
Betamethasone is a steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.
This incurable, always-fatal disease of cattle causes abnormal behavior and trouble walking, with symptoms that may take four to five years to appear after infection — what is this disorder called?
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), commonly known as mad cow disease, is an incurable and always fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle.
Sole living family in the mammalian suborder Tylopoda, which group unites camels with llamas and their South American relatives?
Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
This class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed body segments called proglottids into the environment to infect new hosts — what is this class called (scientific name)?
Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes).
This anatomical term for the hollow between a woman's breasts was coined in its modern sense by a Hollywood censor reviewing the 1943 film starring Jane Russell — what is the term?
Cleavage (breasts) is the narrow depression or hollow between the breasts of a woman.
This group of related RNA viruses causes respiratory illnesses ranging from the mild common cold to deadly diseases like SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what's this virus family called?
Coronavirus are a group of related RNA viruses that cause diseases in mammals and birds.
Nicknamed for the material that made up most of its airframe, this British twin-engined combat aircraft of World War II was one of the fastest operational planes of 1941. What aircraft is this?
De Havilland Mosquito was a British twin-engined, multi-role combat aircraft, introduced during the Second World War.
This C-shaped first section of the small intestine connects the stomach to the jejunum and is the body's principal site for absorbing iron — what is it?
Duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.
This Italian-American physicist won the 1938 Nobel Prize, built the world's first artificial nuclear reactor (Chicago Pile-1), and is called the "architect of the nuclear age" — who was he?

Enrico Fermi (29 September 1901 - 28 November 1954) was an Italian-American physicist, renowned for being the creator of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, the Chicago Pile-1, and a member of the Manhattan Project.
Home to seven living cat species, from the tiny black-footed cat to the jungle cat, and the wild ancestor line of the housecat, which genus of felines is this?
Felis is a genus of small and medium-sized cat species native to most of Africa and south of 60 latitude in Europe and Asia to Indochina.
Most common in the hands and feet, this cold-exposure injury can lead to complications like hypothermia or compartment syndrome — what is it called?
Frostbite is an injury to skin or other living tissue that is allowed to freeze, especially affecting the fingers, toes, nose, ears, cheeks and chin.
This 1984 period drama imagines a bitter rivalry between an 18th-century Vienna composer and his jealous rival, who resolves to ruin the genius's career. What film is it?
Glyphosate (IUPAC name: N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine) is a broad-spectrum systemic herbicide and crop desiccant.
Though usually grouped with the birch family, some botanists split this deciduous shrub genus into its own family — and its nut is a popular snack — which plant?
Hazel are plants of the genus Corylus of deciduous trees and large shrubs native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere.
Named for a Greek youth beloved by Apollo and slain by a jealous wind god who then transformed him into this fragrant spring bloom — what flower genus is it?
Hyacinth is a genus of bulbous herbs and spring-blooming perennials.
This Belgian-American physicist-mathematician and 1992 MacArthur Fellow is best known for harnessing wavelets to compress images — a tool so foundational it bears her name. Who is she?
Ingrid Daubechies (doh-bə-SHEE; born 17 August 1954) is a Belgian-American physicist and mathematician at Duke University.
This British chemical engineer founded and leads a global chemicals conglomerate in 1998, and was briefly the richest person in the UK before shifting his tax residence to Monaco. Who is he?
Jim Ratcliffe (born 18 October 1952) is a British billionaire, chemical engineer, and businessman.

First described in 1845 by a German physicist, these two fundamental equalities govern how current and voltage behave in an electrical network, building on Georg Ohm's earlier work — what are they called?
Kirchhoff's circuit laws are two equalities that deal with the current and potential difference (commonly known as voltage) in the lumped element model of electrical circuits.
This German-born American businessman founded the first company to manufacture blue jeans, launching his San Francisco firm in 1853 — who is he?
Levi Strauss (STROWSS; born Lb Strau,; February 26, 1829 - September 26, 1902) was a German-born American businessman who founded the first company to manufacture blue jeans.
Over a 55-year career this American botanist bred more than 800 plant varieties, from the Shasta daisy to the Santa Rosa plum and a spineless cactus for cattle — who was he?

Luther Burbank (March 7, 1849 - April 11, 1926) was an American botanist, horticulturist, and pioneer in agricultural science who developed more than 800 strains and varieties of plants over his 55-year career.

This prehistoric proboscidean's molars have ridge-like zygodont cusps very different from a mammoth's, and its genus diverged from elephant ancestors over 28 million years ago in the Oligocene — which animal?

Mastodon (from Ancient Greek (masts) 'breast' and (odos) 'tooth') is a member of the genus Mammut (German for 'mammoth'), which was endemic to North America and lived from the late Miocene to the early Holocene.

Introduced in 1975 and still in production today at two Russian factories, this Soviet-designed helicopter family serves as both a medium twin-turbine transport and, in gunship form, an armed attack aircraft — what's the helicopter?

Mil Mi-17 (NATO reporting name: Hip) is a Soviet-designed Russian military helicopter family introduced in 1975 (Mi-8M), continuing in production as of 2024 at two factories in Russia, in Kazan and Ulan-Ude.

This symbiotic relationship between a fungus and a plant, in which fungal threads interconnect with plant roots at the cellular level, plays a major role in plant nutrition and soil chemistry — what is it called?
Doubling as a hormone, neurotransmitter, and neuromodulator, this catecholamine's very name nods to the kidney — and goes by 'noradrenaline' nearly everywhere outside the United States. What is it?

Norepinephrine (NE), also called noradrenaline (NA) or noradrenalin, is an organic chemical in the catecholamine family that functions in the brain and body as a hormone, neurotransmitter and neuromodulator.
Often silent at first, this disease arises from an ovary or nearby structures and announces itself only later with bloating, pelvic pain, and abdominal swelling — what is it?
Ovarian cancer is a cancerous tumor of an ovary.

A Chinese singer famous for annual appearances on a widely watched Lunar New Year television gala, she has served as her country's First Lady since 2012 as the wife of its paramount leader — who is she?

Peng Liyuan (pinyin: Png Lyun; born 20 November 1962) is a Chinese singer who has served as the First Lady of China since 2012, as the wife of Xi Jinping, the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and paramount leader of China.
Which condition, more common in people with obesity or a family history, involves hair and skin debris being drawn into tissue through tiny skin openings called pits?
Pilonidal disease is a type of skin infection that typically occurs as a cyst between the cheeks of the buttocks and often at the upper end.
Used to disinfect both healthcare workers' hands and patients' skin before and after surgery, this antiseptic can be applied as a liquid, ointment, or powder — which compound?

Povidone-iodine is an antiseptic used for skin disinfection before and after surgery. Povidone-iodine (PVP-I), also known as iodopovidone, is an antiseptic used for skin disinfection before and after surgery.
Used to treat malaria and babesiosis, this medication also gives tonic water its distinctive bitter taste — what is it?
Quinine is a medication used to treat malaria and babesiosis. While sometimes used for nocturnal leg cramps, quinine is not recommended for this purpose due to the risk of serious side effects.
One of the U.S. Air Force's three strategic bombers, this supersonic swing-wing aircraft hauls a 75,000-pound payload and answers to the affectionate name 'Bone' — what is it?
Rockwell B-1 Lancer is a supersonic variable-sweep wing, heavy bomber used by the United States Air Force.
This condition gives the spine an irregular S- or C-shaped curve with a twist, and is often compared with kyphosis and lordosis — what is it?
Scoliosis (pl.: scolioses) is a medical condition in which the spine has an irregular curve in the coronal plane, associated with a rotational component.
The brightest star in the night sky, this star sits in the constellation Canis Major and is actually a binary system paired with a faint white dwarf companion — name the star?
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, located in the southern constellation of Canis Major.
This round, gram-positive germ lives harmlessly on most people's skin and noses, but turn opportunistic and it triggers abscesses, sinus infections, and food poisoning. What is it?

Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive spherically shaped bacterium, a member of the Bacillota, and is a usual member of the microbiota of the body, frequently found in the upper respiratory tract and on the skin.

A leguminous tree bearing edible brown pod-like fruits with sweet, tangy pulp, indigenous to tropical Africa and naturalized in Asia, its wood and seed oil have varied uses from cuisine to traditional medicine. What is this tree?
Tamarind (Tamarindus indica) is a leguminous tree bearing edible fruit that is indigenous to tropical Africa and naturalized in Asia.
This herb is also called common thyme or garden thyme and belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae — which species is it?
Thymus vulgaris (common thyme, German thyme, garden thyme or just thyme) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.

This genus of giant theropod dinosaur, whose best-known species takes a Latin name meaning 'king,' roamed an island continent that is now western North America at the very end of the Cretaceous period — name the genus?

Tyrannosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur. The type species Tyrannosaurus rex (rex meaning 'king' in Latin), often shortened to T. rex or colloquially T-Rex, is one of the best represented theropods.
Named after the Scottish engineer who improved the Newcomen steam engine in 1776, this SI unit of power equals one joule per second — what is it?
Watt (symbol: W) is the unit of power or radiant flux in the International System of Units (SI), equal to 1 joule per second or 1 kgm2s3.

This teenage prodigy's work on solvable polynomials helped birth what's now called group theory, and his fiery Republican politics landed him in prison before a fatal duel ended his life at 20 — who was he?
Évariste Galois (25 October 1811 - 31 May 1832) was a French mathematician and political activist.
Recognizable by its black-and-white striped legs and a lyre-shaped marking on its thorax, this mosquito native to North Africa spreads dengue and yellow fever worldwide — what is it?
Aedes aegypti: Species of mosquito. The mosquito can be recognized by black and white markings on its legs and a marking in the form of a lyre on the upper surface of its thorax.
This German polar researcher proposed in 1912 that the continents were slowly drifting apart, a theory mainstream geology only accepted decades later thanks to palaeomagnetism — who was he?
Alfred Wegener: German climatologist and geophysicist (1880–1930)

Inspired by Ørsted's 1820 discovery that current creates a magnetic field, this principle relating a magnetic field's circulation to the current passing through a loop was later generalized by Maxwell with a displacement current term — which physics principle?
Ampère's circuital law: Concept in classical electromagnetism.
Nicknamed 'Nastia' in the USSR and known to NATO as 'Curl,' this twin-engine turboprop military transport was later license-built in China under a different name — what aircraft is it?
Antonov An-26: Soviet turboprop transport aircraft. It is the third member of the Antonov An-24 family, coming after the An-24 and An-30, while preceding the An-32 and cancelled An-132.
Caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides and spread through food tainted with eggs, this infection most often hits children and is symptomless in over 85% of cases — what is it?
Ascariasis: Disease caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. The eggs hatch in the intestines, the larvae burrow through the gut wall, and migrate to the lungs via the blood.
Squat-bodied and built for digging, this group includes the European, ferret, honey, and American species despite not truly sharing one family tree — what are they?
This steroid medication treats everything from rheumatoid arthritis to psoriasis, and can even be given to speed a premature baby's lung development before birth — what is it?
Betamethasone: Steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.
A twinjet successor to a trijet predecessor, this American narrow-body airliner entered commercial service with Eastern Air Lines on New Year's Day 1983. Which aircraft?
Its name means 'thunder lizard,' and though long dismissed as just another sauropod genus, a 2015 study restored this dinosaur's status as distinct — which one?
Brontosaurus: Genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaur. In subsequent years, two more species of Brontosaurus were named: B. parvus in 1902 and B. yahnahpin in 1994.
Which mammal family includes dromedaries, llamas, alpacas, and vicuñas among its seven living species?
Camelidae: Family of mammals. Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
Publishing a landmark 1912 paper on 'vital amines,' this Polish biochemist helped pioneer the concept now known as vitamins while researching pellagra and rickets — who is he?
Capable of sprinting up to 104 km/h, this spotted big cat is the fastest land animal alive, sporting black tear-like streaks down its face and a flexible spine built for speed — which animal?
Cheetah: Large feline of the genus Acinonyx.
Sold under the brand name Biaxin, this macrolide antibiotic treats everything from strep throat to H. pylori infections by slowing bacterial protein synthesis — what is it?
Clarithromycin: Antibiotic medication. Clarithromycin, sold under the brand name Biaxin among others, is an antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections.
Greenish-brown above and off-white below, this migratory leaf warbler is named onomatopoeically for its simple two-note song — which bird?
Common chiffchaff: Small migratory passerine bird found in Europe, Asia and north Africa.
Also nicknamed the prairie wolf, this adaptable North American canine fills a similar ecological niche to Eurasia's golden jackal and was first spotted in Panama in 2013 — what is it?
Coyote: Species of canine native to North America.

Affecting about half of all adults and often treated with antifungal cream, this common scalp condition causes flaking and mild itchiness but isn't actually caused by poor hygiene. What condition is it?
Dandruff: Skin condition of the scalp. It can result in social or self-esteem problems.

Driven by a gradient in chemical potential, this stochastic process describes the net movement of particles from areas of higher to lower concentration and can even reverse direction in spinodal decomposition — what physical process is this?
Diffusion: Transport of dissolved species from the highest to the lowest concentration region.
Defined in humans as an adult height of four foot ten or shorter, this condition's most common form — accounting for about 70% of cases — is a genetic disorder called achondroplasia. What is it?
Dwarfism: Small size of an organism, caused by growth deficiency or genetic mutations.
Nicknamed the ALX, this Brazilian turboprop light-attack aircraft is assembled in Jacksonville, Florida with an American defense partner for low-threat counter-insurgency missions — which aircraft?
Embraer EMB 314 Super Tucano: Light ground attack and training aircraft.
Odorless, colorless, and dangerously sweet-tasting, this viscous compound goes into polyester fibers and antifreeze — and has even been spotted in outer space. What is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Fluconazole: Antifungal medication. Fluconazole, sold under the brand name Diflucan among others, is an antifungal medication used for a number of fungal infections.
Named in 1753 from Greek words for 'milk' and 'flower,' this genus of about 20 bulbous perennial species is better known by its common name, snowdrop — what is its scientific genus?
Galanthus: Genus of flowering plants in the family Amaryllidacee.
The only venomous lizard native to the United States, this sluggish reptile from the Southwest rarely poses a real threat despite its fearsome reputation — what is it?
Gila monster: Largest species of lizard in the United States.

Despite its name, this marine reptile's shell ranges from olive to black — its nickname actually comes from the color of the fat beneath its carapace, built up from an all-plant diet — which species is this?
Green sea turtle: Species of large sea reptile. The dorsoventrally flattened body of C. mydas is covered by a large, teardrop-shaped carapace; it has a pair of large, paddle-like flippers.

Made by fusing heavy nuclei in tiny quantities, this superheavy element 108 has a special isotope whose "magic numbers" of protons and neutrons make its deformed nucleus unusually stable — what is it?
Hassium: Chemical element with atomic number 108 (Hs)

A Greek physician and philosopher of the classical era, this figure is hailed as the "Father of Medicine" for championing prognosis, clinical observation, and the now-discredited theory of bodily humors — who is he?
Hippocrates: Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE)
Though phylogenetically closer to cats, these African carnivores resemble dogs thanks to convergent evolution, and their family has just four living species — what animal is it?
This probability principle holds that a randomly typing creature, given endless time, would almost surely reproduce the complete works of Shakespeare — what's it called?
Infinite monkey theorem: Counterintuitive result in probability.

A Manhattan Project veteran, this American physicist won a share of the 1975 Nobel Prize for proposing that not all atomic nuclei are spherical — an idea later confirmed by Aage Bohr and Ben Mottelson. Who was he?
James Rainwater: American physicist. Rainwater joined the physics faculty at Columbia in 1946, where he reached the rank of full professor in 1952 and was named Pupin Professor of Physics in 1982.
Dubbed the 'Angel of Death,' this German physician held doctorates in both anthropology and medicine before joining the SS and selecting Auschwitz prisoners for the gas chambers — who was he?
Josef Mengele: Nazi SS doctor at Auschwitz (1911–1979)

Also called 47,XXY, this chromosome anomaly leaves those affected phenotypically male but often infertile, and is named after the American endocrinologist who first identified it in the 1940s — what's the condition?
Its lens-shaped seeds, usually two to a pod, are split and simmered into the dal that's a staple across the Indian subcontinent — which legume?
Lentil: Species of plant with edible seeds.
This four-engine American turboprop can land on dirt strips and unprepared runways, then moonlight as a gunship, a flying firefighter, or a weather scout — which versatile workhorse is it?
Lockheed C-130 Hercules: American military transport aircraft.

With a fruiting body resembling an open umbrella, this fungus often grows in fairy rings across Eurasian pastures and is prized as a good edible despite resembling toxic look-alikes — what's its scientific name?
Macrolepiota procera: Species of fungus. Macrolepiota procera, the parasol mushroom, is a basidiomycete fungus with a large, prominent fruiting body resembling a parasol.
In 2014 this Stanford mathematician became the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal, honored for her work on the geometry of Riemann surfaces — who was she?
Patented in 1922 and later marketed as Novalgin or Analgin, this painkiller's sale is restricted in some countries due to a rare blood-cell risk called agranulocytosis — what is it?
Metamizole: Medication. Metamizole or dipyrone is a painkiller, spasm reliever, and fever reliever drug.
This industry extracts everything from coal and gemstones to rock salt and gravel from the Earth, but is also linked to land degradation and habitat loss — what is it?
Mining: Extraction of valuable minerals or other geological materials from the Earth.
In this autoimmune disease the immune system attacks myelin, the insulation around nerve cells, so the central nervous system can't transmit signals properly — what condition?
Multiple sclerosis: Disease that damages the myelin sheaths around nerves.
Also called roundworms, these mostly free-living animals have a tubular digestive tract with openings at both ends and are grouped with arthropods in the clade Ecdysozoa — what are they?
Named for the daring Doolittle airmen of World War II, this subsonic stealth flying wing is being built to replace the B-1 and B-2 by 2040 — which aircraft is it?
Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider: American stealth bomber aircraft.

This dental specialty treats misaligned teeth and jaws, a condition worldwide diets of softer foods have made even more common by leaving smaller jaws with less room to fit them. What specialty is it?
Sold under the brand name Paxil, this SSRI antidepressant treats conditions from panic disorder to PTSD, and is also prescribed for premature ejaculation and menopausal hot flashes — what is it?
Paroxetine: SSRI antidepressant. It has also been used in the treatment of premature ejaculation, and hot flashes due to menopause.
In mathematics, what term describes both an ordered arrangement of a set's members and the act of rearranging them, as seen in the six possible orderings of three distinct numbers?
Permutation: Mathematical version of an order change.
Scientifically named Cajanus cajan, this perennial Fabaceae legume is a staple crop across the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean — what is it?
Pigeon pea: Species of perennial legume. The pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) is a perennial legume from the family Fabaceae native to the Eastern Hemisphere.
Though they look like dolphins, these small toothed whales are actually closer kin to narwhals and belugas, with flat spade-shaped teeth instead of dolphins' cone-shaped ones — what are they called?
